## Introduction: Five Questions About a Coupled Swing

A golfer's earlier actions establish the posture, velocities, activation and
elastic deformation from which later motion develops. Current muscle forces,
gravity, contact reactions and equipment dynamics then act on that evolving
state. The scientific question is how these contributions interact to produce
an impact state, and which changes remain feasible before impact.

Nonlinear control theory helps organize that question, but several different
claims must be kept separate:

1. **Acceleration:** How does a specified input change the instantaneous state
   derivative or clubhead acceleration at a common state?
2. **Energy:** Which mechanisms add, remove, store or redistribute mechanical
   energy over a declared system boundary?
3. **Intervention:** What trajectory follows from changing one input while
   retaining the stated plant, internal states, contacts and external loads?
4. **Finite-Time Control:** Which impact states can bounded inputs actually
   reach within the available time?
5. **Identification:** Which of those quantities can the available measurements
   distinguish, and with what uncertainty?

These questions are intertwined. An earlier torque changes a later state, and
therefore the later drift and torque effectiveness. A contact constraint changes
both acceleration and reaction forces. A model that reproduces a trajectory can
still misattribute the forces that produced it. A locally effective torque may
have little time to change clubhead position, and a large local acceleration
contribution need not add energy to the system.

The purpose of the affine formulation is to make such distinctions calculable.
It does not establish that the golf swing is universally drift dominated, that
muscles supply only small corrections, or that proximal braking is an optimal
coaching strategy. The examples below are analytical illustrations, not fitted
human-swing results.

## From Mechanical Loads to State Rates

For a smooth mechanical model in independent local coordinates, take
$v=\dot q$ and write

$$
M(q)\dot v+h(q,v,t)=B(q,t)u.
$$

The coordinates include every retained rigid and flexible mechanical degree of
freedom. The inertia matrix $M$ is positive definite on these independent
coordinates. The term $h$ groups the loads moved to the left of the equation:
velocity-dependent terms, gravity, retained elastic and dissipative terms, and
any specified external loading with the appropriate sign. The input convention
is part of the model. In an effective joint-torque model, $u$ contains the
selected generalized actuator torques and $B$ maps them into the force balance.

When this mechanical state is complete, stacking $x=(q,v)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x,t)&=\begin{bmatrix}v\\-M^{-1}h\end{bmatrix},\\
G(x,t)u&=\begin{bmatrix}0\\M^{-1}Bu\end{bmatrix},\\
\dot x&=f(x,t)+G(x,t)u.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $Bu$ is a generalized load, $M^{-1}Bu$ is an acceleration contribution,
and $G(x,t)u$ is a **state-rate contribution**. They cannot be substituted for
one another. Force and torque are conjugate to displacement and angle;
position-rate and acceleration blocks also have different units. Any norm that
mixes those blocks needs an explicit scaling convention.

The displayed state is insufficient when retained physics has memory. Muscle
activation, tendon history variables, controller states or hysteresis variables
must then be included in $x=(q,v,z)$ with their evolution equations. The enlarged
system is control affine only if its full derivative is affine in the declared
instantaneous input at fixed complete state. An excitation input can enter an
activation equation while the existing activation continues to generate muscle
force. Conversely, a model with input-dependent stiffness at fixed state may
fail to admit the stated affine split. An additive equation is an assumption to
justify, not a physiological validation result.

Generalized velocities need not equal coordinate derivatives globally; other
representations require $\dot q=N(q)v$. Redundant coordinates require constraint
handling. The equations in this section use the stated independent-coordinate
chart, rather than treating it as a universal human-body parameterization.

### Contact Changes the Acceleration Map

For a stationary ideal holonomic constraint with Jacobian $J(q)$, a redundant
coordinate description instead solves

$$
\begin{aligned}
M\dot v+h&=Bu+J^T\lambda,\\
J\dot v+\dot Jv&=0.
\end{aligned}
$$

The reaction $\lambda$ is solved together with acceleration. After solving this
system in a feasible fixed mode, the input-to-acceleration map generally differs
from the unconstrained $M^{-1}B$. Moving supports need the corresponding explicit
time terms. Unilateral contact also requires checking the sign of the normal
reaction, friction feasibility and the appropriate transition when the assumed
mode ceases to apply.

A ground reaction is consequently not automatically an independently commanded
input. In a whole-body contact model it can be an output of the constrained
dynamics. In a reduced segment model a measured ground or grip wrench may be a
prescribed external load. Both are possible conventions, but they answer
different intervention questions. The [force-measurement article](technology-force-measurement.qmd)
and [induced-acceleration chapter](The_Physics_of_Golf/quarto/ch30b_induced_acceleration.qmd)
develop these boundaries.

## Drift Is Instantaneous; the State Reflects Earlier Action

Let $\Phi_0(t,t_0,x_0)$ be the solution of the declared zero-input system. Along
that solution,

$$
\frac{d}{dt}\Phi_0(t,t_0,x_0)
=f\bigl(\Phi_0(t,t_0,x_0),t\bigr).
$$

The right-hand side must be evaluated at the evolving state. To recover
$f(x_0,t_0)$, evaluate the derivative at the initial time. Drift is an
instantaneous vector field; the forward zero-input trajectory is its evolution
through time. A complete state summarizes the information needed to predict
future evolution under the model. It need not encode a recoverable record of
the entire past, and different histories can lead to the same state.

Earlier muscle action can increase velocity, stretch a tendon or bend a shaft.
Those changes alter the state at which the later drift is evaluated. Hence
independence from the **current** input at fixed state does not imply
independence from previous inputs along a trajectory. This is the precise sense
in which preparation and later natural motion are connected.

Writing $F$ for the full state derivative, input affinity at a common state gives
the identity

$$
F(x,u,t)-F(x,0,t)=G(x,t)u.
$$

If a reference and a zero-input branch have reached different states, their
rate difference additionally contains the difference between their drift
fields. Subtracting two separated trajectories is therefore a finite
intervention comparison, not a pointwise isolation of the current input term.
The [canonical ZTCF treatment](zero-torque-counterfactual.qmd) distinguishes
pointwise evaluations, stitched evaluations along a reference, forward branches
and velocity-reset diagnostics.

### Zero Input Is a Declared Intervention

A forward counterfactual is reproducible only after specifying the plant,
parameters, complete initial state, input channels, retained schedules,
constraints, external loads and event rules. Within a smooth mode, suitable
regularity such as local Lipschitz continuity in the state supplies local
uniqueness. It does not guarantee global existence or feasible continuation
through every possible contact event.

Zero generalized joint torque, zero muscle excitation and zero activation are
three different interventions. Zero net joint torque does not imply absent
antagonistic muscle forces. Setting a new excitation command to zero does not
instantaneously erase activation or tendon strain. A torque-level model cannot
identify that underlying physiological decomposition without further modeling
and evidence.

The zero-velocity counterfactual is similarly a model evaluation after a stated
reset of selected velocity variables, usually combined with zero selected input.
It is not an instrument or an independent measurement of load. Gravity, retained
elastic forces, activation and scheduled external loads can remain. A reset must
also satisfy constraints; setting velocity to zero may be incompatible with a
moving support. Its value is a defined comparison, not a universal passive-force
or muscle-effort reading.

### Coordinate Changes Preserve an Intervention; Input Offsets Change It

For a smooth invertible state transformation $y=\Psi(x)$, held within its chart
and suppressing explicit time arguments,

$$
\dot y=D\Psi(x)f(x)+D\Psi(x)G(x)u.
$$

If the same physical input and all other model choices are preserved, the
zero-input solution transforms to the same physical motion. This covariance
does not select a unique physiological baseline. It also does not equate models
with different constraints, flexible states, parameters or omitted forces.

For a configuration transformation $y=\psi(q)$, acceleration contains an
additional term:

$$
\ddot y=D\psi(q)\ddot q+D^2\psi(q)[v,v].
$$

For example, $y=q^2$ on the chart $q>0$ gives
$\ddot y=2q\ddot q+2v^2$. Transforming only the acceleration vector by the
Jacobian would miss the velocity-squared term.

Changing the input origin is a different operation. If
$u=\alpha(x)+\beta(x)w$, then

$$
\dot x=\bigl(f+G\alpha\bigr)+G\beta w.
$$

Zero $w$ generally applies a nonzero physical $u=\alpha(x)$. Feedback
linearization or an equilibrium torque offset can therefore change what a
"zero-input" trajectory means. A free system with a purely kinetic Lagrangian has
geodesic motion under its kinetic metric; adding gravity, dissipation, elastic
loads or contacts requires the corresponding forced or constrained dynamics.
The general human-club baseline should not be called a geodesic without those
qualifications.

## Underactuation, Coupling and Local Authority

Underactuation concerns the accelerations that a declared input map can
produce, not the visual complexity of a motion. In the unconstrained mechanical
model, the acceleration set at a fixed state is

$$
\mathcal A(x,t)
=\left\{-M^{-1}h+M^{-1}Bu:\ u\in\mathcal U(x,t)\right\}.
$$

With unrestricted inputs, rank deficiency of $B$ relative to the independent
mechanical degrees of freedom prevents arbitrary instantaneous accelerations.
Counting inputs is sufficient to detect some deficiencies but is not the full
criterion: extra channels can be dependent, and contact can change the relevant
space. Even a full-rank map with bounded inputs produces a limited acceleration
set. Human muscle redundancy, a floating base, foot contacts and flexible
coordinates must be assessed within a specific model.

MIT's [underactuation introduction](https://underactuated.mit.edu/intro.html)
formulates the issue through achievable acceleration and input constraints.
That framework does not imply that drift must be large. A horizontal two-DOF
inertial model with only its first coordinate actuated is underactuated, yet at
rest with no other loads its drift is zero. Conversely, a fully actuated system
can have large gravitational or velocity-dependent loads relative to its
actuator bounds.

For a task point with position $r(q)$ and Jacobian $J_r$, unconstrained
acceleration is

$$
\ddot r=J_r\bigl(-M^{-1}h+M^{-1}Bu\bigr)+\dot J_rv.
$$

The local torque-to-task-acceleration map is $J_rM^{-1}B$; the complete drift
part also includes $\dot J_rv$. In a rigid torque-driven model, $M$ and $B$ may
depend only on configuration, even though the drift depends strongly on
velocity. Broader muscle or flexible models can introduce additional state
dependence. The same torque can then affect different task directions and
magnitudes as posture changes.

A drift-control ratio can summarize a specified projected magnitude relative
to a declared input set. It does not retain every directional property of
$\mathcal A$, and it does not specify how the set evolves before impact. A large
ratio is neither a proof of lost control nor a measurement of the muscular
share of effort. See the [DCR treatment](controllability-drift-ratio.qmd).

## Inertial Coupling Without Energy Amplification

### A Coupled Acceleration Balance

Partition independent coordinates into proximal and distal groups. The distal
row of the unconstrained mechanical equation is

$$
M_{dd}\ddot q_d
=(Bu)_d-h_d-M_{dp}\ddot q_p.
$$

All gravity, velocity-dependent, elastic and other retained bias terms belong
in $h_d$. The term $-M_{dp}\ddot q_p$ explains a coupling contribution after
rearranging the equation; it is not by itself a separately measured anatomical
joint reaction or proof of a particular amount of energy transfer. The complete
proximal and distal equations must be solved together.

For a two-coordinate positive-definite inertia matrix,
$M_{pp}>0$, $M_{dd}>0$ and $M_{pp}M_{dd}-M_{pd}^2>0$. An arbitrary large coupling
coefficient can violate this requirement and permit negative kinetic energy.
Moreover, inertias in kg m² multiply angular accelerations expressed in rad/s²,
not unconverted numerical values in deg/s².

Physical interactions between connected segments are transmitted through their
joint forces and moments. The mass matrix encodes that mechanical geometry in
the chosen coordinates. Its off-diagonal entries can change under coordinate
transformations; an individual entry or ratio is not a coordinate-independent
energy-transfer efficiency.

### Worked Example: A Braking Torque in the Two-Rod Teaching Model

Use the illustrative two uniform rods from the
[Chapter 6 worked example](The_Physics_of_Golf/quarto/ch06_zero_torque_counterfactual.qmd):
$m=(2,0.2)$ kg, $L=(0.4,0.3)$ m, COMs at $L/2$, COM inertias $mL^2/12$, and
$g=9.81$ m/s². The fixed base lies in a vertical plane; $q_1$ is measured
counterclockwise from horizontal and $q_2$ is the second rod's angle relative to
the first. There are no elastic, frictional or moving-support loads in this
example. These are teaching parameters, not identified torso or club inertias.

At $q=(45,70)$ degrees and $v=(8,12)$ rad/s, the coupled inertia is

$$
M\approx
\begin{bmatrix}
0.152875150&0.010104242\\
0.010104242&0.006000000
\end{bmatrix}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}.
$$

Its eigenvalues are approximately $0.005308140$ and $0.153567010$ kg m², both
positive. The complete zero-input acceleration, including velocity and gravity
bias, is

$$
\ddot q_0\approx
\begin{bmatrix}11.699484\\-119.253631\end{bmatrix}
\ \mathrm{rad/s^2}.
$$

Apply a proximal braking torque $u=(-2,0)$ N m at that same state. Solving the
full matrix equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta\ddot q=M^{-1}u
&\approx\begin{bmatrix}-14.721123\\24.790964\end{bmatrix},\\
\ddot q=\ddot q_0+\Delta\ddot q
&\approx\begin{bmatrix}-3.021639\\-94.462667\end{bmatrix}
\quad\mathrm{rad/s^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The distal acceleration **increment** is positive, while its total relative
acceleration remains negative. A positive contribution is not the same as
positive total acceleration. Nor is $q_2$ the absolute distal orientation:
$\theta_2=q_1+q_2$. Its input acceleration increment is the sum of the two
components, $10.069841$ rad/s². Declaring relative versus absolute
angles matters even in this small model.

This calculation establishes a local effect at one state. It does not show
that braking increases distal speed at a later impact. That requires a complete
trajectory comparison with matched initial conditions, bounded inputs and a
declared endpoint or event rule. Calling a torque "braking" also refers to its
power at the current velocity; its sign alone is insufficient.

### The Energy Ledger

For a time-independent mechanical model with conservative potential $V$,
viscous or other dissipative generalized force $d$, and external generalized
load $Q_{\rm ext}$, write

$$
M\dot v+C v+\nabla V+d=Bu+Q_{\rm ext}.
$$

With a consistent Coriolis representation satisfying the mechanical energy
identity, $E=\tfrac12v^TMv+V$ obeys

$$
\dot E=v^TBu+v^TQ_{\rm ext}-v^Td.
$$

Stationary ideal constraint reactions do no work on admissible velocities.
Moving supports, contact slip, impacts and internal energy states require their
own power or event accounting. The equation is a balance across a stated
boundary, not a declaration that all biological work is measured by net joint
power.

In the two-rod example, the sole actuator power is
$v^Tu=8(-2)+12(0)=-16$ W. An independent finite difference of the complete kinetic
plus gravitational energy along the calculated state derivative also gives
$-16$ W. The braking input removes mechanical energy while changing the distal
acceleration contribution. There is no energy amplification by the coupling
matrix. Gravity or stored elasticity can release previously stored potential
energy, while muscles or external actuators can supply new work.

A segment-level energy balance additionally includes powers of forces and
moments crossing that segment's boundary. Coordinate-wise kinetic-energy terms
are not automatically segment energies, because the quadratic form contains
cross terms. To identify energy flowing into the club, use its physical body
energy and interface wrench powers in consistent frames.

Angular momentum has a separate balance involving external moments about a
specified point. Negative actuator power alone does not establish whether total
angular momentum is conserved; a support reaction can affect momentum even when
it does no work. Consequently, correlated proximal slowing and distal speeding
cannot by themselves identify the source, amount or efficiency of energy
transfer.

## Geometry and Control Before Impact

### Accessibility Is Different From Small-Time Local Controllability

Accessibility asks whether a locally reachable set has an interior. Small-time
local controllability requires the starting state to lie inside the locally
reachable set for arbitrarily short positive horizons while remaining in a
sufficiently small neighborhood. The input set and permitted motions matter.
An algebraic span of vector fields is not, by itself, a finite-time performance
result for a system with drift and bounded actuators.

A scalar counterexample makes the distinction explicit:

$$
\dot x=1+u,\qquad |u|\le\tfrac12.
$$

Its vector fields span the one-dimensional state space, and reachable intervals
have nonempty interiors. Nevertheless, $\dot x\ge1/2$, so no admissible input
moves the state left from its starting value. It is not small-time locally
controllable there. A large enough opposite input would change the conclusion,
which is why the actuator set belongs in the claim.

For a driftless system with reversible inputs, noncommuting control flows can
generate additional directions. For instance, let
$g_1=(1,0)$ and $g_2=(0,x)$ on a plane. The sequence $+g_1,+g_2,-g_1,-g_2$, each
applied for time $\epsilon$, returns the first coordinate to its start and
changes the second by $\epsilon^2$. With the convention

$$
[g_1,g_2]=Dg_2\,g_1-Dg_1\,g_2,
$$

the bracket is $(0,1)$. This example shows a direction generated by a sequence,
with a second-order displacement and a total time $4\epsilon$. It does not
provide an instantaneous independent actuator in that direction. A system with
drift that cannot be reversed does not automatically permit the same four-flow argument.

The publisher-hosted *Modern Robotics* treatments of
[local reachable sets](https://modernrobotics.northwestern.edu/nu-gm-book-resource/13-3-2-controllability-of-wheeled-mobile-robots-part-2-of-4/)
and the
[driftless rank condition](https://modernrobotics.northwestern.edu/nu-gm-book-resource/13-3-2-controllability-of-wheeled-mobile-robots-part-4-of-4/)
make the admissible controls explicit. Applying such tools to a golf model
requires its actual fields, constraints and bounds. Lie brackets can be useful
in studying controllability, but their existence does not prove that a named
proximal-to-distal sequence is necessary or improves impact speed.

### Instantaneous Gain Is Only One Ingredient of a Finite-Time Effect

Linearize a smooth control-affine model along a feasible reference
$(\bar x(t),\bar u(t))$. For small perturbations within the same mode,

$$
\delta\dot x=A(t)\delta x+G(\bar x(t),t)\delta u,
$$

where $A$ includes both the state derivative of $f$ and the derivatives of the
input fields weighted by the reference inputs. If $\Phi(T,t)$ is the transition
matrix of this variational system, then

$$
\delta x(T)=\Phi(T,t_0)\delta x(t_0)
+\int_{t_0}^{T}\Phi(T,s)G(\bar x(s),s)\delta u(s)\,ds.
$$

This expression connects present authority to later outcomes through the
intervening dynamics. MIT's
[trajectory-linearization discussion](https://underactuated.mit.edu/lqr.html)
uses a moving reference, not just a stationary equilibrium. The approximation
must be checked against nonlinear trajectories; contact events require event
and reset sensitivity, and an impact-defined endpoint can shift in time.

Even the double integrator illustrates the importance of duration. For
$\ddot q=u$, $|u|\le a$, compare trajectories with equal initial position and
velocity against zero input. At a fixed horizon $T$,

$$
|\Delta q(T)|
=\left|\int_0^T(T-s)u(s)\,ds\right|
\le\tfrac12aT^2.
$$

A saturated constant input attains this bound. Halving the available time
quarters the possible position correction, despite unchanged instantaneous
acceleration authority. High speed does not make geometry irrelevant; it makes
actual horizons, bounds, delays and the evolving state indispensable.

### Geometric Phase Is a Specific Mechanism

A geometric-phase claim needs a specified symmetry or group motion, shape
variables and a reconstruction rule connecting a shape cycle to net motion.
Kelly and Murray's
[author-hosted abstract](https://murray.cds.caltech.edu/Geometric_Phases_and_Robotic_Locomotion)
describes that framework for robotic locomotion. It does not demonstrate a golf
sequencing effect. A swing is not automatically a closed shape cycle, and a
change in clubhead position is not sufficient evidence of geometric phase.

Inertial coupling already explains how joint accelerations interact in a
mechanical model. A phase-based explanation may add insight for an appropriately
specified model, but it must identify what it predicts beyond that force
balance. The linked governed critique remains open: its concern about conflating
coupling with nonholonomic steering is relevant, while its own categorical
full-actuation and efficiency statements also need model-specific support.

## What the Other Control Tools Can Establish

### Partial Feedback Linearization

For a selected smooth position output $y=r(q)$, one can often write
$\ddot y=b_y(x)+A_y(x)u$ within a fixed mode. Prescribing an output acceleration
requires the relevant rank condition on $A_y$, a feasible input solution and
attention to the internal dynamics left after controlling the output.
Saturation, singular postures and model error can prevent the intended
cancellation. The
[MIT cart-pole and Acrobot treatment](https://underactuated.mit.edu/acrobot.html)
illustrates why collocated and noncollocated outputs have different conditions.
This tool helps analyze a chosen task; it does not establish that a golfer's
nervous system implements exact nonlinear cancellation.

### Optimal Control and Energy Shaping

An optimal-control study must state a terminal objective, a running cost,
initial conditions, duration, dynamics and admissible trajectories. For example,

$$
\min_{u(\cdot)}\left[
\phi(x(T))+\int_{t_0}^{T}\ell(x(t),u(t),t)\,dt
\right]
$$

is incomplete until input, state and contact constraints are supplied. Different
weights on impact speed, accuracy, effort or tissue loading can produce
different policies. Squared net joint torque is a chosen penalty, not generally
a metabolic-energy measurement. A numerical local optimum is not automatically
a global optimum or a description of human behavior.

Energy shaping is a particular feedback-design idea: the controller changes
closed-loop dynamics to obtain a desired energy structure. It is not synonymous
with any redistribution of energy in a swing. Neither underactuation nor an
optimal-control formulation guarantees that optimal inputs are small
perturbations. Feasibility, actuator limits and the chosen objective can require
substantial input throughout a maneuver.

### Observability and Unknown-Input Identification

Classical observability asks whether internal states can be distinguished from
outputs over time under a specified model and known input. An unknown torque is
an input unless a model explicitly augments it as a state with dynamics. Adding
that state is an additional assumption, not a free reconstruction of a missing
measurement.

For example, if only $\dot x=d+u$ is observed and both $d$ and $u$ are unknown,
the same measured derivative can be explained by increasing $d$ and decreasing
$u$ equally. A control-affine label does not resolve this ambiguity. In a swing,
kinematics may constrain effective joint torques only after inertial properties,
external loads, contact and derivative estimation are specified. Net torque
still does not uniquely determine individual muscle forces or co-contraction.

Sensor selection should therefore be linked to an explicit distinguishability
question. Ground forces, grip wrenches, kinematics and shaft measurements observe
different boundaries and states. Noise, timing offsets, parameter uncertainty
and derivative filtering can further limit an otherwise identifiable model.

### Robustness and Data-Driven Identification

A sensitivity calculation asks how a prediction changes with parameters or
perturbations. A robust guarantee requires a defined uncertainty set and a
specified property, such as feasibility or an impact-error bound, across that
set. A stable nominal linearization does not establish robustness throughout a
nonlinear swing or across a contact transition.

Learning $f$ and $G$ from data likewise requires sufficient input information
and variation. If only one unknown-input trajectory is observed, different
splits can fit it. Physics constraints, calibrated inputs, held-out interventions
and uncertainty analysis can reduce ambiguity; they must be evaluated for the
quantity the article interprets. Good trajectory fit alone is insufficient
evidence of correct force attribution.

## A Research Program That Connects the Questions

A useful study starts with a falsifiable question, such as whether a specified
proximal torque change increases a declared clubhead speed component at a
specified event. The following sequence connects mechanics to evidence:

1. **Declare the Plant and Boundary.** Specify coordinates, retained flexible
   and physiological states, input channels, contacts and measurement frames.
   Document which loads are measured, modeled, prescribed or solved reactions.
2. **Verify the Mechanics.** Check inertia definiteness, units, complete force
   balance, energy and momentum accounting, and convergence. Preserve the same
   physical intervention under coordinate changes.
3. **Compare Defined Interventions.** Match initial complete states and retained
   schedules. Report both pointwise acceleration differences and forward
   trajectory outcomes, including event timing and feasibility failures.
4. **Assess Finite-Time Alternatives.** Apply input, rate, delay and state bounds.
   Examine the task directions that remain reachable and the sensitivity to
   uncertain parameters, rather than inferring authority from one scalar ratio.
5. **Test Identification and Prediction.** Determine whether the sensors can
   distinguish the proposed mechanisms. Compare against independent measurements
   or held-out interventions with uncertainty and alternative explanations.

Equipment comparisons must also specify what is held fixed. Replaying identical
torque, imposing identical kinematics and allowing an adapted control policy
are different experiments when shaft properties change. A conserved quantity
under zero input must be derived for the declared loads and constraints; a
learned near-constant on one trajectory is only a candidate invariant.

Hybrid motion can be studied, but requires explicit modes, guards, reset maps
and a well-posed continuation rule. Counterfactual branches may encounter
different events. A fixed-contact calculation should stop or change mode when
its contact assumptions fail, rather than extrapolating an impossible reaction.
No physical participant test or golf-specific optimal policy is established by
this article's analytical examples.

<details class="technical-explanation">
<summary>In Layman's Terms</summary>

Earlier action prepares the moving body and club. Later action then works with
that moving state. A mathematical baseline asks what a specified model would do
if a specified input were changed. It does not erase the effort that prepared
the state, and it does not measure a universal percentage of the swing supplied
by muscles.

A braking torque can change how the links accelerate while removing energy from
the entire system. That is why "the torso slowed while the club sped up" is an
observation to explain, not proof of a beneficial braking strategy. The complete
motion, the forces crossing segment boundaries and the time left before impact
all matter.

The same reasoning applies to control. A torque that strongly affects
acceleration may arrive too late to change position much. A model that predicts
motion well may still assign the wrong causes when inputs or contact forces are
unknown. Carefully defined comparisons and independent measurements connect
these pieces into a testable explanation.

</details>

<details class="technical-explanation">
<summary>Critics' Comments</summary>

**Does a torque-level model establish physiology?** No. It can be useful for a
declared mechanical question while omitting activation-dependent stiffness,
co-contraction and tissue history. Its predictions need validation at the
level being interpreted; a net-torque result is not an individual-muscle result.

**Does the coupled example establish a sequencing prescription?** No. It verifies
one local input effect and its energy accounting in a specified two-rod model.
A useful golf intervention requires a matched finite-time comparison and
appropriate empirical evidence. Neither coupling nor Lie brackets alone supply
that result.

**Does qualification make the framework unfalsifiable?** It should do the
opposite. Declare the model and predicted output before comparison, preserve
failed and null results, and test alternatives. A model-dependent claim can be
precise; an unrestricted assertion about all swings cannot be rescued by moving
its assumptions after observing the outcome.

**Does this rewrite resolve the governed critique?** The existing critique stays
visible and open. Correcting the exposition is distinct from adjudicating a
scientific claim against its required evidence. This article does not claim a
95% skeletal-baseline accuracy result or a uniquely physiological zero input.

</details>

was accessible; its full preprint was unavailable during this review. No video
timestamp or video-content claim is made here. The two-rod values and the
control counterexamples are independently checked analytical examples, not
reproductions of a published human dataset.
